references.text: Just two verses earlier, the rulers also mock Jesus with similar words: 'He saved others; let him save himself' (Luke 23:35). The soldiers' mockery in verse 37 repeats this motif but focuses on his royal title.
The soldiers who mock are the same ones mentioned in Luke 23:36, where they come forward and offer him vinegar as part of their overall mockery.
The inscription above Jesus' cross read 'This is the King of the Jews' (Luke 23:38). The soldiers' taunt 'Are you the King of the Jews?' directly connects to this inscription.

In Matthew's parallel account, passersby and chief priests mock Jesus with similar words: 'Save yourself! ... He saved others; let him save himself if he is the Christ, the chosen one' (Matthew 27:40-42).
Mark's parallel describes the same mockery at the cross, where passersby and chief priests say: 'Save yourself and come down from the cross! ... He cannot save himself' (Mark 15:29-32).
John tells of the inscription 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' (John 19:19-22). The title 'King of the Jews' is central to the soldiers' mockery in Luke 23:37.

The devil tempted Jesus with the words 'If you are the Son of God...' (Luke 4:3). The structure 'If you are ... then save yourself' in 23:37 reflects the logic of that temptation, where Jesus is challenged to prove his identity through an act of power.
During the mockery before the crucifixion, the soldiers hailed Jesus as 'King of the Jews' (Matthew 27:29). The same ironic use of the royal title is repeated at the cross.
The soldiers struck Jesus and said, 'Hail, King of the Jews!' (John 19:3). The title 'King of the Jews' is consistently used mockingly by the soldiers, including here in Luke 23:37.
During his trial before Pilate, Jesus was asked: 'Are you the King of the Jews?' (Luke 23:3). The soldiers' mockery at the cross builds directly on this charge raised during the trial.
